To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

increases and decreases of the force requirements for response initiation have different effects on temporal response differentiation, and that the effects of drugs depend on the direction of the changes in force requirements.

the accuracy with which rats respond for a reinforcer for a specified time interval is determined by the relative frequency of response durations that meet the reinforcement requirement, and that drugs affect response-duration differentiation by altering the relative frequency of different response durations.

increases and decreases of response-force requirements produce different changes in temporal accuracy, and that the effects of PCPs on temporal accuracy are not the same as those produced by increases in response force requirements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of drugs on the accuracy of timing and response differentiation.
the effects of drugs on the ability of rats to make fine discriminations between durations of behavior.

the effects of drugs on the ability of animals to discriminate between durations that are close in magnitude but that are separated by a criterion that is not based upon absolute duration, but rather on the relative frequency distribution of response durations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the accuracy of temporal differentiation is affected by changes in response force requirements, but that the nature of this effect is different from the effects of changes in response time requirements.

the accuracy of temporal-response differentiation is affected by the response force requirements in such a way that increases in force requirements decrease timing accuracy and decreases in force requirements have the opposite effect.
increases in force requirements for lever-press responses decrease the accuracy of temporal discrimination and produce a shift toward shorter response durations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of drugs and other manipulations on response-force requirements are not simply additive or subtractive to the effects of drugs on timing accuracy.
the effects of a drug on response-duration differentiation depend on the type of task, the reinforcement contingency, and the force requirements for response execution.

increases in response force requirements produce increases in response durations to meet reinforcement criteria, but decreases in force requirements produce decreases in response durations to avoid the production of reinforcement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of drugs on temporal discrimination are highly context-dependent.
the force requirement for lever pressing is an important determinant of the accuracy of response-duration differentiation.
increases in response-force requirements for lever pressing are more disruptive of timing accuracy than are decreases in the force required to operate the lever.
